item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q004_ferritin_like_functional_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places all three in the all-alpha ferritin-like fold (a.25), but not at the same evolutionary level. Ferritins and ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins are separate families within the ferritin-like superfamily (a.25.1), supporting remote homology despite divergence from iron oxidation/storage to radical generation or other dinuclear-metal chemistry. Manganese catalases form the separate manganese-catalase superfamily (a.25.2); their shared a.25 architecture alone does not establish common ancestry with a.25.1 and may reflect only a broadly similar four-helix-bundle solution. Consequently, ferritin function must not be transferred to RNR-like proteins, and neither sequence annotations nor catalytic mechanisms should be transferred between a.25.1 and manganese catalases. Structure templates across these groups can support fold recognition and coarse core alignment, but not metal identity, catalytic residues, substrate specificity, oligomeric state, or function. Representatives should be selected separately by family—and separately by superfamily for manganese catalase—using experimentally characterized, complete structures rather than one protein as a functional proxy for the whole fold. Specific assignments require external biochemical evidence such as metal/cofactor analysis and activity assays, supplemented by conserved active-site residues, sequence-profile/phylogenetic evidence, oligomeric structure, and genomic context.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
